statement: A triangle has its corners at the points (1, 1), (7, 3) and (3, 9). What is its area?

choices.misconception: I used the coordinate formula for the area correctly but forgot to halve at the end.
I assumed the triangle covers exactly half of the 6 by 8 rectangle around it.
I worked out the three right-angled triangles around the outside and gave their total instead of subtracting it from the rectangle.
I gave the area of the 6 by 8 rectangle that surrounds the triangle.

hints: Draw the smallest rectangle, with sides along the grid lines, that contains the triangle.
Box the triangle in a rectangle, then cut away the right-angled triangles in the corners. Check the answer with a second method, such as the shoelace formula.
The rectangle runs from x = 1 to 7 and from y = 1 to 9, so it is 6 by 8. The three corner triangles have areas 6, 12 and 8.

solutions.reliable: The smallest rectangle around the triangle has opposite corners (1, 1) and (7, 9), so it measures 6 by 8 and has area 48. Inside the rectangle but outside the triangle are three right-angled triangles: below the side from (1, 1) to (7, 3), with shorter sides 6 and 2 and area 6; to the right of the side from (7, 3) to (3, 9), with shorter sides 6 and 4 and area 12; to the left of the side from (3, 9) to (1, 1), with shorter sides 2 and 8 and area 8. So the triangle has area 48 - 26 = 22. A second method as a check: the shoelace formula gives half of |1(3 - 9) + 7(9 - 1) + 3(1 - 3)| = half of |-6 + 56 - 6| = 22. The transferable idea: when two independent methods agree, you can mark the answer with confidence.

whyOnTest: Checking with a second method catches slips like a forgotten half: box-and-subtract and the shoelace formula must agree.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
